privacyQ: Is my file sent to a server?
privacyA: No. The file is read locally and processed with the Melt renderer in your browser. The page can download application code and the optional example image, but it does not upload your selected media.
outputImageA: Choose PNG for a lossless image, JPEG for a compact photograph, or WebP when supported. The longest output edge is capped at 1920 pixels and smaller sources are not enlarged. The ASCII treatment is exported visually, not as a text file.
outputVideoA: Choose automatic encoding, MP4 or WebM. Supported codecs depend on your browser. The selected clip can be up to 60 seconds, at 30 fps, with up to 1920 pixels on its longest edge. Audio is included when enabled and present in the source.
controlsQ: Can I change the look after I choose a file?
controlsA: Yes. The effect stays adjustable while you preview. Change its parameters, compare the source and result, and download again. The source file is not modified. Your selection is released when you leave the tool.

ascii.name: ASCII
ascii.summary: Turn photographs into grids of characters, from fine typographic detail to bold blocks of text.
ascii.about: ASCII art builds an image from characters instead of a smooth surface. Melt samples the brightness of each cell and uses its own glyph atlas to draw denser or lighter symbols. The result is rendered by the same TSL effect used in the studio. Color mode keeps tones from the source; monochrome produces a restrained typographic image. Choose image tones, shaded ink, solid ink or a two-color gradient with an adjustable angle.
tips: Use smaller characters to preserve faces and small details.
Increase the cell size for a bold poster or a deliberately abstract result.
Mix in a little of the original with the Amount control for a softer treatment.
ascii.question: Does the ASCII converter export editable text?
ascii.answer: This tool creates a visual ASCII treatment and exports an image or video. The characters are rendered as part of the picture, rather than a plain-text document. Use the character-size and color controls to shape the look before downloading.

dither.name: Dither
dither.summary: Reduce images to a black-and-white or source-color palette with ordered pixel patterns.
dither.about: Dithering represents tones with patterns from a limited palette. Choose multilevel Bayer, fixed threshold, Bayer 2 × 2, Bayer 4 × 4, Bayer 8 × 8 or interleaved noise. Multilevel Bayer also exposes the number of tonal levels. Source colors processes each source RGB channel; turn it off to use your ink and paper colors. Contrast, gamma and pattern strength refine the result.
tips: Start with Bayer 4 × 4 for a balanced, recognizable pattern.
Choose foreground and background colors with enough separation.
Use a larger pattern scale for a chunky print-inspired texture.
dither.question: What is the difference between threshold and Bayer dithering?
dither.answer: Threshold makes a direct light-or-dark choice. Binary Bayer distributes those choices with an ordered matrix to suggest intermediate tones; Multilevel Bayer retains more tonal levels. With Source colors off, the result uses your ink and paper palette. With it on, each RGB channel is processed separately.

halftone.name: Halftone
halftone.summary: Give photography and footage a dotted, print-inspired surface with an adjustable dot size.
halftone.about: Halftone uses a regular dot treatment to reinterpret the source image. In Melt, the cell size controls the scale of the printed texture, Amount mixes the treatment with the original, and Color chooses between a colored and monochrome result. It is useful for editorial images, textured posters, cover art and graphic motion backgrounds.
tips: Try a larger dot size for imagery viewed at a distance.
Use a smaller size when a face or product needs to stay recognizable.
Compare colored and monochrome versions before choosing the final treatment.
halftone.question: Can I adjust the halftone dots without resizing my file?
halftone.answer: Yes. The effect’s scale changes its dot grid independently of the output-size setting. You can test a fine or coarse pattern while keeping the same output dimensions. The preview uses the same effect parameters as the downloaded result.

cyanotype.name: Cyanotype
cyanotype.summary: Create a blue photographic-print treatment with ink, paper, exposure and texture controls.
cyanotype.about: Cyanotype is inspired by the characteristic blue-and-paper appearance of photographic prints. Melt recreates that visual treatment digitally: exposure and contrast shape the subject, ink and paper colors define the palette, and texture controls add wash, unevenness, grain, fibers and edge fade. It is a digital effect, not a chemical printing process.
tips: Adjust exposure first so the subject is readable.
Change ink and paper together to keep a coherent palette.
Use subtle grain and wash when you want the photograph to remain the focus.
cyanotype.question: Can I change the blue and paper colors?
cyanotype.answer: Yes. Ink Color, Paper Color, density, wash, texture, fibers and edge treatment are directly available in the parameter panel. All settings use the same local cyanotype effect as the full Melt editor.

crt.name: CRT
crt.summary: Add scanlines, display masks, curvature and glow for a retro screen treatment.
crt.about: A CRT-inspired filter changes the appearance of the display rather than simply laying stripes over the picture. Melt combines a configurable screen mask, scanlines, curvature, convergence and glow. All display and tonal controls are available in the parameter panel. Try it on typography, artwork, game imagery or a short video clip.
tips: Keep scanlines subtle when the source contains small text.
Use curvature and glow sparingly for a cleaner retro display.
Compare the available mask patterns to find a texture that suits the subject.
crt.question: Is CRT the same as a VHS filter?
crt.answer: This converter focuses on a retro display treatment: screen masks, scanlines, curvature and glow. It does not claim to simulate every aspect of an analog tape workflow. The result is a stylized digital effect that you can adjust with Melt’s controls.

posterize.name: Posterize
posterize.summary: Simplify continuous tones into fewer color levels for graphic, poster-like artwork.
posterize.about: Posterization reduces the number of tonal levels used to represent an image. Lower levels create broad, clearly separated color regions; higher values retain more subtle transitions. Melt’s Amount control blends the quantized image with the source. This makes the tool useful for graphic studies, social assets and footage that benefits from a flatter, more illustrative look.
tips: Begin with six levels, then lower the value for a stronger graphic look.
Increase the level count when skin tones or gradients become too harsh.
Use Amount to blend the treatment instead of changing the original file.
posterize.question: Does posterization use the same process as dithering?
posterize.answer: No. Posterization quantizes colors into a smaller number of levels. Dithering distributes a limited palette into patterns to suggest intermediate tones. They produce different textures; try the related Dither converter when you want a visible pixel pattern.
